1a) Worship of the Śakti Pavilion (śaktimaṇḍapapūjā)
I bow to Gaṇanāyaka, whose face is swarmed by bees intoxicated by the fragrance of his temples,
for the sake of attaining the goal of Śiva’s teachings.
Now, the procedure for the worship of the Śakti-sacrifice is described.
Having adorned the sacrificial hall with pavilions, sacrificial pits, archways, pillars, waves, strings of pearls, and so forth,
and having decorated it with faith and other virtues, [the officiant] should, according to the rules, [place] rice in the center of the altar—

Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with rice grains, sesame seeds, and parched grain, [one should fashion] the *pradhānavardhanī*, the *vidyeśvaravardhanī*, and the *parivāravardhanī* according to the prescribed characteristics. Having performed the sprinkling of the altar with water mixed with sesame and barley, and having offered incense, one should adorn it with water, blood, mango leaves, coconut, new cloth, and fragrant substances.
Having installed the retinue and the Vardhanīs from the eastern direction up to the northeast, the Guru,
having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), [worships] Mahāśānti, Gaṇeśa, Brāhmī, Bhānu, Maheśvarī, Skanda, Vidyā, Mahāśāstā, Kaumārī, and Vāstunāyakī.
Vaiṣṇavī, Ramā, Vṛṣabhā, Nivṛttikā,
Vīrabhadra, Varāhī, Māyā, and likewise Māhendrikā.
Mohinī, Kṣetrapāla, and likewise Pratiṣṭhā; Caṇḍeśvarī, Cāmuṇḍī, Astra, and Astreśvarī;
as well as Gurudurgā, Bhāratī, and Gaurī—these are proclaimed in the sacrifice.
Bhānu, Śāntimat, Danti, Vidyā, Skanda, and the Teacher;
Pratiṣṭhā, Kṣetra, Caṇḍeśī, Nivṛtti, and likewise Vṛṣabha; Vīrabhadra, Āvidhi, Māyā, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Picā.
Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Gaurī, Māhendrī, Caṇḍī, Durgikā, Bhāratī, Lakṣmī, Mohinī, and likewise the form of the Guru—
one should worship all the deities from Sūrya up to the Guru.

Having entered the interior of the sacrificial hall through the western door, the preceptor— having adorned himself with new garments, fine silk (*dukūla*), perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains on his head, as well as makara-shaped earrings, necklaces, armlets, a waist-thread, golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a rosary of *rudrākṣa* beads, and so forth— and having taken his place in the southwest (*nirṛti*) direction, shall worship Gaṇapati, perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited.

Being pure, one should sprinkle everywhere. Having worshipped the Śiva-sūrya [image] daily between the directions of Indra and Agni [the southeast], [one should recite]: *oṃ hāṃ arkāsanāya namaḥ*; *oṃ khaṃ khaṣolkāya śivasūryamūrttaye namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*): One should meditate upon the Sun—shining like saffron, two-eyed, single-faced, and seated upon a lotus; holding a lotus, an *amara* [flower], and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands, and a lotus in his left hand... [joined] with Pratyūṣā or with Śobhā, who is likewise adorned. One should meditate on him as red, wearing fragrant garlands and garments, radiant with a halo of light.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ, obeisance to Śivasūrya. Having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and so forth, the Guru, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual application of sacred ash according to rule, prepares the general *arghya* offering. Having sprinkled the archway at the eastern gate with the *astra-mantra* and shielded it with the *kavaca-mantra*, he offers obeisance to the center of the archway: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Peaceful Archway (*śāntitoraṇa*).
[It is] adorned with blue garments and unguents, two-armed, with palms joined in *añjali* and holding a lotus.
One should meditate upon Śāntitoraṇa, who has a formidable face and is dark-complexioned. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śāntitoraṇa*—(p.7a, f.2b, l.1)—to the Lord of Śāntitoraṇa;
*oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhadra*—above.
Dark-complexioned, with two eyes, one face, and four arms, bearing a staff, a rosary, the *Ṛgveda*, and joined palms—homage! Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the *Ṛgveda*;
oṃ, homage to the Kṛta Age; on the tridents: oṃ, homage to the Gaṅgā; oṃ, homage to the Yamunā; oṃ, homage to the Narmadā.

On the northern and southern branches: *oṃ indrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śacīdevyai namaḥ*. At the base of the northern branch: *oṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ svāhādevyai namaḥ*. At the base of the southern branch: *oṃ hrīṃ bhūrlokāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ pratyuṣāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ somāya namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ bhuvarlokāya namaḥ*;
*oṃ hrīṃ prabhāsāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ bhaumāya namaḥ*. [And] on the northern threshold (*vardhanī*) of the door.

[One should meditate upon] Śānti, who has four faces and four arms, is white in color, possesses great strength, and holds a banner, an axe, a rosary, and a lotus; she wears the sacred thread across all her limbs. (Verse 6) Oṃ Hrīṃ Namaḥ.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the Door of the Śāntikalā. On the upper lintel (udumbara), in the northern and southern sections: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Sarasvatī! Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Mahālakṣmī! Peace in the northern pitcher:
one-faced, two-eyed, and adorned with a crown and a casket.

One should meditate upon Śānti, who has the luster of the color of a blue cloud, holds a fan, and has a crow as his vehicle; he is the son of Chāyā. *Oṃ hrīṃ śanaiścarāya namaḥ* [is placed] in the southern pitcher at the door.
One should meditate upon Gaṇapati, who has the face of an elephant, three eyes, a dark complexion, and four arms;
holding a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*) and an axe (*paraśu*) in his left hands, and a tusk and a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in his right hands;
adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and decorated with all ornaments. *Oṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. (L. 4)
Having offered the food offering, incense, and lamps, [one should worship] on the upper banner of the door:
"He is peaceful, red in color, two-armed, and two-eyed;
his hands are joined in the gesture of reverence, and he is adorned with various ornaments. (l. 5)
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Praśānta. On the southern banner is Śiśira, red in color, with two arms and two eyes;
his hands are joined in the añjali gesture, and he is adorned with various ornaments. (Verse 6)
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Śiśira. One should visualize the white-colored lily on the upper banner of the door in the eastern quarter;
it has two eyes, two arms, and is endowed with a staff and the gesture of fearlessness.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kumuda. At the door: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Weapon-Gatekeeper. Oṃ hriṃ, obeisance to the *avarga* group; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the *kavarga* group.

Having offered the *arghya* with the mantra "Svāhā to all the gatekeepers," and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should say]: "You must remain as the protectors of this sacrifice."
Having thus informed those who were intent on his welfare,
[he saw] Kumudākṣa in the southeast— the direction of fire— on the banner of the southeast, possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
with two eyes, two arms, and holding a staff and the gesture of fearlessness. (l.4)
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kumudākṣa.
Having sprinkled the southern door-arch with the weapon-mantra and veiled it with the armor-mantra, [one should meditate] in the middle of the arch upon [the deity] who has two arms,
two eyes, and is adorned with black ornaments.
The Bhūtitoraṇa is described as having a thick neck and a large belly. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Bhūtitoraṇa;
salutation to Vijaya, the lord of Bhūtitoraṇa.
He is red in color, has two eyes, and wears a white sacred thread.
One should visualize the Yajurveda as having become a handful of sacrificial grass (*sṛggaṇḍikā*). Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Yajurveda.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Tretā Age. Upon the tridents: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Sindhu River; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Godāvarī River.

On the eastern and western branches: *oṃ hrīṃ yamāya namaḥ*. To Kāḷakaṇṭhī, *namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ niṛṛtaye namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ jātāya namaḥ*. At the base of the eastern branch: *oṃ hrīṃ suvarlokāyai namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ ajaghanyai namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ budhāyai namaḥ*. At the base of the western branch: *oṃ hrīṃ maharlokāyai namaḥ*.
*oṃ hrīṃ jaghanyai namaḥ*. *oṃ hrīṃ bṛhaspataye namaḥ*. In the pitcher at the front of the door.
He has three faces—red, white, and the crescent moon—and four arms; he holds a rosary, a lotus, and a book that resembles a blazing fire.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the door of the Vidyā-kalā.
On the upper *udumbara* beam, in the eastern, western, and central sections: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati;
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. [This is] in the eastern jar of knowledge (*vidyā*).

I worship the one born from Rudra, whose vehicle is the peacock; he has the luster of coral, a single face, and is all-pervading; his hands hold a thunderbolt, a spear, and grant the boons of generosity and fearlessness; he is the slayer of the enemies of the world of gods and the bestower of freedom from obstacles.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Skanda. In the western pitcher of the door:
[one should visualize him] with a vast body, dark-blue and tender, clothed in variegated garments, and holding a red lotus in his left hand.
I take refuge in the Teacher, who wears a lofty crown of jewels, whose crest is the Lord of the Planets (Rāhu), and whose face is pleasing.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to the son of Hari and Hara! Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should place it] on the eastern banner at the entrance.
Parjanya is red in color, two-armed, and two-eyed;
his hands are joined in the añjali gesture, and he is adorned with various ornaments.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Parjanya; on the western door-pendant. (L.5) Jayanta is white in color, two-armed, and two-eyed;
his hands are joined in the añjali gesture, and he is adorned with various ornaments. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jayanta; on the banner above the door. (L.6)
One should visualize Puṇḍarīka on the right, having the luster of a bumblebee, with two eyes and two arms, and endowed with a staff and the gesture of fearlessness. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Puṇḍarīka.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the weapon-gatekeepers of the door. Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the *ca*-group. Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the *ṭa*-group. Svāhā to all the gatekeepers. Having thus offered the *arghya*, and having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and *yonimudrā*, and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), incense, lamps, and so forth, one should inform them: "You must remain here as protectors of the sacrifice, maintaining your vigilance. In the banner of the southwest corner (*nirṛti-kona*), in the region of Nirṛti, [one should visualize] Vāmana, who has a luster like crushed collyrium, two eyes, two arms, and holds a staff and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his hands.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vāmanā. Having sprinkled the northern door-arch with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should worship the Arch of Health in the center of the arch: two-armed and two-eyed, with long hair hanging on both sides, and a face formidable with fangs. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the Arch of Health.
To the Lord of the Archway of Health: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Nīlalohitā. Above:
White in color, with two eyes, and wearing a golden sacred thread;
joined with the staff of the Brahmāstra, he is the Sāmaveda with palms joined in reverence.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Sāmaveda. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Dvāpara Yuga. On the tridents: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Kāverī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Godāvarī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Triveṇī. On the two door-posts of the western gate: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Kāverī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Gambhīrā.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Harṣiṇī. At the base of the western branch: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Janaloka. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Prabhañjanā. (l. 4) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhārgavā. At the base of the eastern branch: [obeisance] to Tapoloka. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pratāpa. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara. (l. 5) In the western pitcher at the door: [one who is] like pure crystal, having two faces and four arms.
[She] holds a noose, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a rosary, and a lotus, and is adorned with jewels of stability (*pratiṣṭhā*). Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the door-deity Pratiṣṭhākalā.
On the upper *udumbara* beam, in the western, eastern, and middle sections: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. (l.2) In the western consecration jar: [one should meditate on] the one whose brilliance is like sapphire, who has a form of wrath and is terrifying, with fangs bared, hair standing erect, and holding a staff and a trident in his hands.
Holding a skull and a serpent in his hands, having the form of a Kṣetrapāla:
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapālā. [This is] in the eastern jar at the entrance.
He has one face and two eyes, and is adorned with a crown and a casket;
he holds an utpala lotus in his right hand and displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) with his left hand.
He wears earrings on his ears and is decorated with all [types of] ornaments.

With the right foot extended and the left foot drawn in, one should perform the worship of Gaurī, who is the fruit of service; then one should worship Dhātrī and Caṇḍeśvarī. [Recite: *oṃ hrīṃ caṇḍeśvaryai namaḥ*. Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth—
On the western door-banner:
Dhanada is red in color, with two arms and two eyes;
his hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture, and he is adorned with various ornaments.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dhanadā. (L.2) On the eastern banner at the entrance: Śrīprada is white in color, two-armed, and two-eyed;
his palms are joined in reverence, and he is adorned with various ornaments. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīpradā. In the central lotus.
With a pleasant face and resembling a bee, he is situated in the direction of Kubera;
he has two eyes and two arms, and is endowed with the gestures of the staff and fearlessness.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sumukhā. At the door: obeisance to the weapon-mantra goddess, the guardian of the entrance. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the *tavarga* group of consonants. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the *pavarga* group of consonants. Svāhā to all the guardians of the entrance. Having thus offered the *arghya*, and having displayed the *dhenumudrā* and *yonimudrā*, and having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should inform them: "You must remain here with due diligence as the protectors of this sacrifice."
On the banner in the northeast corner: Īśāna, well-established, with a luster white as the moon, two-eyed and two-armed, endowed with a staff and the gesture of fearlessness.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Supratiṣṭhā. Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should sprinkle the archway at the western gate with the Astra-mantra and enclose it with the Kavaca-mantra. In the center of the archway [one should meditate on the deity] who is red in color, two-eyed, and has a serpent as his sacred thread.
I meditate upon Balatoraṇā, who is endowed with joined palms in *añjali* gesture.
Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Balatoraṇā, the sovereign of Balatoraṇā. Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vajrā. [Above:
Black, four-armed, three-eyed, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣasūtra*).
And one should worship Atharvaṇa, who holds his hands together in the *añjali* gesture, with: *oṃ hrīṃ atharvaṇavedāyai namaḥ*.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Kaliyugā. On the tridents: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Śoṇabhadra; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Bhāgīrathī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Tuṅgabhadra. (L. 2) On the southern and northern branches: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Varuṇa; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Bhoginī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vāyavī. (L. 3) Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Ghorashakti. At the base of the southern branch: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Satyaloka; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Āvāhanā.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Rāhu. (L. 4) At the base of the northern branch: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dhṛvalokā; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vivāhā; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ketu. (L. 5) In the southern pitcher at the western door: She has the luster of molten gold, is adorned with a single face and the moon, and is celebrated as Nivṛtti, holding a vajra, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus.

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Nivṛttikalādvārā. On the upper *udumbara* beam, in the southern, northern, and middle sections: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī. In the southern pitcher of Nivṛtti:
[one should worship] a bull, white in color, with sharp horns and great strength.

Having meditated upon the form of Dharmadeva with both feet joined together and one foot standing outside, as well as his vehicle, the bull— with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ vṛṣabhāya namaḥ*— in the northern jar at the door.

[One should meditate on him] as fierce, an incarnation of Rudra, with eyes like fire, hair standing erect, possessing fine tusks, with limbs reaching to the sky, of terrifying form, and shining like a thick, dense cloud.

I bow to Vīrabhadra, the sole hero of the world, who is dark as the earth, whose limbs are encircled by garlands of bells, who is the sovereign lord of *bhūtas* and *pretas*, and who bears a lofty leaf made of gold. Oṃ Viṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra.
Having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, [one should worship] at the southern banner of the door.
Red in color, Bhūtasañjīvana has two arms and two eyes;
his hands are joined in the *añjali* gesture, and he is adorned with various ornaments. OṂ HRĪṂ, homage to Bhūtasañjīvana! [He is located] on the northern banner of the gate.
Amṛta is white in color, two-armed, and two-eyed;
his palms are joined in *añjali*, and he is adorned with various ornaments.
(l.3) Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Amṛtasañjīvana. [He is] on the banner above the door.

[Vāruṇya] and Śaṅkhukarṇa, resembling the asterisms of the quarters, having two eyes and two arms, and endowed with the *daṇḍa* and *abhaya* gestures: *oṃ hrīṃ śaṅkhukarṇāya namaḥ*. At the door: *astrāyadvārapālāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ yavargāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ ṣavargāya namaḥ*; *sarvebhyo dvārapālebhyaḥ svāhā*. Having thus offered the *arghya*, and having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, the *mahāmudrā*, and the *yonimudrā*, one should worship [them] with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having requested, "You must remain as protectors of the sacrifice with due diligence," [one should place] the serpent-eye in the northwest corner,
conjoined with the Lord of the Stars (the Moon).

Having two eyes and two arms, and endowed with the *daṇḍa* and *abhaya* gestures: *oṃ hrīṃ sarpanetrāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, thereafter, in the directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast: (l. 2)

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Airāvata, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Puṇḍarīka, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vāmana, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kumuda, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Añjali, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Puṣpadanta, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sārvabhauma, the elephant. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Supratīka, the elephant. All of them bear white color, possess two eyes, and are of great strength;

adorned with all ornaments, they are the eight elephants of the directions beginning with the east. Having meditated thus, [one should proceed] immediately thereafter in the directions beginning with the east.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Hetukāma. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Tripuraghna. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vahni. (l.5) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Yamajihva. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kāla. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Karālin. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ekāṅghri. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhīma.
(l.6) Those beginning with Hetukā are proclaimed as having faces made terrifying by fangs, possessing great bellies, and being joined with the *khaṭvāṅga* staff. They are all-knowing.
Again, in the directions starting from the east: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅgabhairava.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Rurubhairava. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍabhairava. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Krodhabhairava. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Unmattabhairava. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kapālabhairava.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Bhīṣaṇabhairava. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Saṃhārabhairava. [These are placed] on the twelve pillars, starting from the east and ending with the northeast. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mananā. (L. 3) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Puruṣā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Tuṣṭā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Rati. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Dhṛti. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śaśinī. (L. 4)
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Candrīkā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kānti. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jyotsnā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrī. On the four pillars starting from the southeast (āgneya):
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vitaraṅgā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇāmṛtā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kāmā. If the sacrificial enclosure is covered with grass and so forth...

At the *kaṃpa*s: *oṃ hrīṃ prithivītattvāyai namaḥ* (Salutation to the Earth-principle); *oṃ hrīṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Sarasvatī, the sovereign of the Earth-principle). At the *triṇa*s: *oṃ hrīṃ jalatattvāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Water-principle); *oṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Mahālakṣmī, the sovereign of the Water-principle). At the *bandha*s: *oṃ hrīṃ agnitattvāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the Fire-principle); *oṃ hrīṃ bhavānyai namaḥ* (Salutation to Bhavānī, the sovereign of the Fire-principle). At the *vaṃśa*s... (line 2)

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the wind principle; obeisance to the sovereign of the wind principle. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Maheśvarī. On the pillars: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the ether principle; obeisance to the sovereign of the ether principle. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī. Having thus meditated upon the pavilion as pervaded by these seats of power (*śakti*), [one should worship] on the pinnacle: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śivā. On the canopies: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Candrikā.

On the waves: *oṃ hrīṃ jāhnavyai namaḥ*. On the garland of *darbha* grass: *oṃ hrīṃ vāsukyai namaḥ*. In the courtyards: *oṃ hrīṃ mudgarāya namaḥ*. (L. 5) In the directions: *oṃ hrīṃ astrāya namaḥ*. Thereafter, in the south-eastern corner: one should visualize the nature of the *kṣetrapāla*, naked, three-eyed, four-armed, holding a noose, a trident, and a skull-cup, with hair standing erect, holding a *ḍamaru* drum, and accompanied by a dog. *Oṃ hāṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ*. Having worshipped thus, and having secured the other doors with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [one should worship] the door-keepers as in the daily rite.

Having worshipped [the deities] at the western gate... then, for the sake of worshipping Gaurī, one should sprinkle the general *arghya* with the *astra-mantra*. Having worshipped the Lord of the Threshold (*dehali-pati*) situated at the eastern gate, immediately thereafter one should worship the power (*śakti*) of the door-guardian on the left side of the door.
And Jayā has the luster of red color, with two eyes and a terrifying form;
her left foot is bent while the right is positioned straight.
She holds a sword in her right hand and is equipped with a shield in her left.

I worship her who stands at the left of the doorway, endowed with fierce fangs, bearing a sword and a shield; her right foot bent and her left standing straight, adorned with all ornaments. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vijayā. (l. 5)

One should begin the worship of the door for those two [deities]. On the upper part of the doorpost, in the southern, northern, and middle sections: *oṃ hrīṃ nirmadāyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. On the southern jamb of the door: *oṃ hrīṃ gaṅgāyai namaḥ*. To its left: *oṃ hrīṃ śivayoginyai namaḥ*. On the northern jamb of the door: *oṃ hrīṃ yamunāyai namaḥ*. To its right: *oṃ hrīṃ bhūtinyai namaḥ*.
On the upper part of the body: *oṃ hrīṃ pataṅginyai namaḥ*. On the lower part of the body: *oṃ hrīṃ bhuvaṅginyai namaḥ*. On the right branch:
*oṃ hrīṃ vegavatyai namaḥ*. On the left branch: *oṃ hrīṃ godāvaryai namaḥ*. On the right door-panel: *oṃ hrīṃ sindhave namaḥ*. On the left door-panel: *oṃ hrīṃ kāveryai namaḥ*.
On the bands: *oṃ skandāya namaḥ*. On the two bracelets: *oṃ sūryāya namaḥ*, *oṃ candrāya namaḥ*. In the hollow: *namaḥ* to the nine powers (*navashakti*). In the base: *oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*. (l.
6) In front of the door: *oṃ vṛṣabhāya namaḥ*; having offered the *arghya* with "svāhā to all the door-keepers," [he places it] on the ground: *oṃ hrīṃ vighnādhyakṣāyai namaḥ*. (p. 16a, f. 11b, l. 1)

Having dispelled the obstacles situated on the ground with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and three strikes of the right heel—[and those] in the intermediate space with the mantra: *oṃ vighnarājāya namaḥ | oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*—by casting flowers with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) and the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*), [one should likewise dispel] the obstacles in the intermediate space. In heaven: *oṃ vighneśvarāya namaḥ | oṃ hrīṃ gaurīyai namaḥ*.

Having cast away obstacles from the sky with the root mantra placed on the thumb and ring finger while looking with the eye, and having requested protection for them, one should enter the interior—taking refuge slightly in the left branch while leading with the right foot—while sounding the bell with the *astra* mantra. On the lower floor, one should resort to the *adhombaraka* with the *prabhañja* weapon. For the purpose of warding off [obstacles] situated in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, [one should recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ astraśaktyai namaḥ*. Thereafter, having informed [the deity], [one should place the offerings] all around in the eight auspicious directions beginning with the east.
To Urvaśī, who holds the Śrīvatsa: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīvatsā; to the sovereign of the Śrīvatsa: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Umādevī. To Menakā, who holds the water-pot (karaka):

Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Karakā; to the sovereign of the karaka: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. To Rambhā, who holds the lotus: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Kamalā; to the sovereign of the lotus: Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Devī.

In the mirror held by Tilottamā: *oṃ hrīṃ darpaṇāyai namaḥ*, to the Mistress of Mirrors; *oṃ hrīṃ kāveryai namaḥ*. (l. 3) In the banner held by Sumukhi: *oṃ hrīṃ patākāyai namaḥ*, to the Mistress of Banners; *oṃ hrīṃ śrīdevyai namaḥ*. In the svastika held by Sundarī: *oṃ hrīṃ svastikāyai namaḥ*, to the Mistress of Svastikas; *oṃ hrīṃ bhadrāyai namaḥ*. In the conch held by Kāmukhī: *oṃ hrīṃ śaṅkhāyai namaḥ*. (l. 5)

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Śacīdevī, the sovereign of the conch; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Dīpā, who holds a lamp that increases desire; oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gaurī, the sovereign of the lamp. Having worshipped thus, thereafter, on the southern side of the altar, seated upon a tortoise-throne or a beautiful seat made of tiger-skin and so forth, facing north, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the placement of the digits of Gaurī (*gaurīkalānyāsa*), the purification of the inner place of worship, the purification of the mantra, and the purification of the substances for the special *arghya* offering, and having performed self-worship (*ātmapūjā*): On this forehead: *Oṃ huṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ*, and to the presiding deity of the Śiva-principle: *Oṃ hrūṃ icchāśaktyai namaḥ*. In the throat: *Hrīṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ*, and to the presiding deity of the Vidyā-principle: *Oṃ hrīṃ jñānaśaktyai namaḥ*. In the feet: *Oṃ hāṃ ātmatattvāya namaḥ*, and to the presiding deity of the Ātman-principle: *Oṃ hrāṃ kriyāśaktyai namaḥ*.

Having performed the placement [of the mantras] in this manner and again effected the process of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and then having performed the internal sacrifice (*antaryajana*) and the fire-oblation (*havana*), and having protected the body by means of the *tālatraya* and other [ritual gestures], one should prepare the special water-offering (*viśeṣārghya*). Having sprinkled that water upon one’s own head, and having sprinkled the entire collection of sacrificial materials with the *kuśa* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should drench them with the *kavaca-mantra*.

Having consecrated [the object] with the heart-mantra, one should transform it into nectar (*amṛtīkuryāt*). Thereafter, together with a pair of garments, a turban, camphor powder, saffron flowers, and fragrant ashes, one should then adorn all the limbs. [One should provide] a golden ring, a bracelet, a waist-band, earrings, and a golden sacred thread—these five ornaments along with the other decorations.
The preceptor, being exceedingly pure, should perform this especially.

Having thus adorned his own body, for the purpose of fashioning the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*), he should place the form of the seat upon the palm of his own right hand, which has been smeared with sandalwood paste and upon the left thumb; then, having placed the pentad beginning with Īśāna upon the fingers from the thumb to the little finger.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *vidyā*, the body, and the eyes, and having invoked Gaurī, one should place the limbs (*aṅga*) in the sequence starting from the little finger and ending with the arrow-finger (*iṣu*). Having rendered [the deity] supreme (*paramīkṛtya*) and meditated upon her in the form of light, one should mount her upon one’s own head. Having shaken off the veil of darkness both internal and external by means of the light that has entered the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and having perceived the quarters of space as fully illuminated, one should hold the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), over which the weapon-mantra (*astra*) has been recited seven times, at the right hip of the preceptor, and having placed the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the southwest (*naiṛtya*).

Then, having consecrated seven times with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* the parched grain (*lāja*), sandalwood, *siddhārtha*, ashes, flowers, *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), or pure parched grain as scattering-offerings (*vikirān*), and having placed them [there], one should thereafter, in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), stand with the upper body erect facing northeast (*aiśāna*) while scattering the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the water offering (*arghya*). Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial hall (*yāgagṛha*) with the *astra* mantra, one should perform the inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and other rites.

Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*)— up to the four-footed [rite]— for the purpose of removing the thorns, one should carry out inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), sprinkling with water (*abhyukṣaṇa*),

digging (*khanana*), scattering (*avakīraṇa*), filling (*pūraṇa*), leveling (*samīkaraṇa*), pouring (*secana*), pounding (*kuṭṭana*), sweeping (*sammārjana*), and smearing (*samālepana*) by means of a sword or *kuśa* grass, accompanied by the ritual branches (*kalās*) beginning with *nivṛtti*.

One should place the primary seed-syllables in the west, north, south, east, and the center; perform the encircling with three lines using the root-mantra; worship with the Īśāna-mantra; draw three lines—one toward the east and one toward the north—using the Astra-mantra; perform the "vajrification" at both ends by means of two *kuśa* blades shaped like tridents, with their tips pointing east and north, using the root-mantra. In this way, one should perform the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). Having thus consecrated the sacrificial site, [one should visualize] various emanations in the form of weapons, purified by the Astra-mantra and blazing forth, ending with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having scattered [the offerings] for the purpose of pacifying obstacles in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and having returned by way of circumambulation from left to right, one should gather [the materials] with a bundle of *kuśa* grass (*kūrca*) using the *Gaurī-gāyatrī* mantra for the purpose of warding off obstacles on the ground.
Having established them in the northeast for the seat of the *Astravardhanī*, one should place the *Vaiṣṇavī* [vessel] in the eastern jar in the southwest.
Brahmā, four-faced, holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a rosary (*akṣamālikā*), is to be meditated upon.

The presiding deity of the Vāstu [should be] mounted upon a swan, with a yellow body; [the mantra is]: *Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the Vāstu*. In the western direction, in the south-eastern corner, [he is] three-eyed, four-armed, and possesses a luster like the *japā* flower.
One should meditate upon Mahāmāyā, who holds a flower-arrow, a sugarcane bow, a noose, and a lotus, and who is clothed in variegated garments. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Mahāmāyā.
In the northeast, to the west of the Guru-kumbha, one should prepare a seat for the Pāśupatāstra-kumbha upon the *vardhanī* and the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using the Vikara weapons.

Upon that, having established the Kumbha and the Vardhanī with its neck facing west, one should prepare a mobile seat within the Kumbha and worship the seat with: "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of the Pāśupatāstra. Then, the meditation: [He is] five-faced, most terrible, ten-armed, three-eyed, deformed, radiant, and fierce.

Having meditated upon the god Pāśupata, who possesses tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair, and whose hands hold a sword, shield, iron arrow, bow, string, water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), spear, trident, axe, and the staff of Brahmā (*brahmadaṇḍa*); the wise one should worship him along with his limbs (*sāṅga*). [Mantra: *oṃ pāśupatāstramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
[Mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Having thus performed the worship beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), etc.—

Then, upon the *vardhanī* vessel, one should worship the seat with: "Oṃ, homage to the one seated upon the power of the *Pāśupata* weapon. Having performed the worship of the seat, one should meditate:
having visualized the Goddess Astrarī, who is red in color, with blazing hair, and holding a sword and a shield, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the power (*śakti*) who is the embodiment of the *pāśupatāstra* weapon; huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. (L.

3) Having thus performed the rites of invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, and having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense, and lamps, one should thereafter worship Brāhmī and the others in the directions beginning with the east. (L.
4) At the southern threshold of the eastern gate—one should worship Brāhmī, who is adorned with yellow garments, seated upon the vehicle of a swan. (L. 5)
Having meditated thus: "Four-armed and two-eyed, endowed with four faces,
[holding] the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), as well as a rosary (*akṣamālā*) and a water-pot (*gaṇḍikā*)," one should worship with perfumes,
flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, saying "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī," and then offer prayers.
"O Brahmī! For the sake of pacifying all obstacles to yourself, you must remain attentive until the conclusion of the sacrifice, by the command of Śiva. Having thus informed her:
In the *vardhanī* vessel for Agni: she has three eyes and four arms, endowed with a white complexion;
she is adorned with a crown of matted hair and possesses a single face;
she bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons, and holds a deer and an axe.
One should meditate upon Māheśvarī as mounted upon her bull-vehicle. Having thus meditated, [one should recite]:
*oṃ hrīṃ māheśvaryai namaḥ*. Having offered perfume, flowers, food offerings, incense, and lamps, and having worshipped and prayed:
"O Māheśvarī, for the pacification of all my own obstacles and calamities..."

"By the command of Śiva, one must remain attentive until the conclusion of the sacrifice. Having thus informed [the deity], the Guardian of the Southern Door is located at the western *vardhanī*. He has one face and two eyes, is dark blue in color and in the prime of youth, endowed with four arms, and possesses two feet.

Having meditated thus: [the goddess] mounted upon a peacock vehicle, adorned with a crown of matted locks, holding a spear and a vajra in her other hands, as well as displaying the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons; and having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should pray: *oṃ hrīṃ kaumāryai namaḥ*.

"O Bhobhoma! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in your own direction, you must remain vigilant until the end of the sacrifice, by the command of Śiva. Having thus addressed Kaumārī, [he addresses] Nairṛtī in the Vardhanī vessel:
"Two-eyed, four-armed, dark-complexioned, and in the full bloom of youth..."

Having meditated thus: "The Goddess who bears the conch and discus, endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, mounted upon the vehicle Garuḍa, and adorned with all ornaments"— and having worshipped her with *oṃ hrīṃ vaiṣṇavyai namaḥ* using perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should pray:
"O Viṣṇu, by you, for the sake of pacifying obstacles on this path,
one must remain attentive until the end of the sacrifice, by the command of Śiva. Having thus informed the Vaiṣṇavī [deity].
At the northern *vardhanī* of the western gate— (l.2) two-eyed, two-armed, peaceful, clad in black and yellow garments,
endowed with the face of a boar, and possessed of a red complexion. (l.3)

Having meditated thus: "She is adorned with a crown and tiara, seated upon a lion, holding a plow and a mace, radiant with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons"— and having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, saying "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī," one should offer prayers.

"O Vārāhī! By your command, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles, you must remain attentive until the end of the sacrifice, by the order of Śiva. Having thus informed Vārāhī, [one should place her] in the *vardhanī* vessel of the northwest—two-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, and endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
Having meditated thus: "She is endowed with a vajra and a spear, possessing a golden-blue form, adorned with a jeweled crown, and mounted upon an elephant vehicle"— *Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Māhendrī*.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, and having made this petition: "O Great Lord, for the pacification of all obstacles beginning with yourself,
you must remain attentive until the end of the sacrifice by the command of Śiva," he should thus inform Mahendra.
And at the northern gate, in the eastern *vardhanī*, is Caṇḍeśvarī— four-armed, three-eyed, with a complexion like a dark cloud,
her face terrifying with protruding fangs, and wearing a tiger-skin garment.
Holding a ketaka thorn and a trident in her hands, and endowed with a skull-cup,
she is adorned with a garland of tinkling bells, wears a crown of karanda flowers, and possesses a parrot; she is encircled by a garland of heads and seated upon a corpse as her vehicle.
Having meditated thus upon her as being adorned with all ornaments, possessing full breasts and in the prime of youth—
Oṃ Hrīṃ, homage to Cāmuṇḍā.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, and having made this request:
"O Cāmuṇḍī, by the command of Śiva, you must remain here attentively until the end of the sacrifice for the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction," thus he should inform Cāmuṇḍī.
On the Vardhanī of Īśāna:
she wears a crown adorned with a conch and a discus, her hands display the gestures of granting fearlessness and resting on the thighs;
she is endowed with all ornaments, possesses full breasts, and is in the prime of youth.
Having meditated upon Śivadurgā—four-armed, three-eyed, beautifully adorned with a dark complexion, and seated upon Mahiṣa—one should recite: *oṃ hrīṃ śivadurgāyai namaḥ*.
Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should offer this prayer:

"O Durgā! For the sake of pacifying obstacles on your behalf, you must remain alert until the end of the sacrifice by the command of Śiva. Having thus addressed Durgā, [he places her] in the southern *vardhanī* of Īśāna.
In the left hand, she holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), as well as a mallet; in the right,
she holds a lotus, endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Having meditated thus on Sarasvatī, the wise one should worship her along with her limbs.

Having meditated thus—*oṃ hrīṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*—and having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, he should pray: "O Sarasvatī, for the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction, by you..."

"By the command of Śiva, one must remain attentive until the end of the sacrifice. Having thus informed Sarasvatī, [he visualizes] Nirṛti in the northern *vardhanī*: two-armed and two-eyed, endowed with a jeweled crown, possessed of a yellow complexion, and beautiful in all her limbs.
Having meditated thus: "In her right hand is a lotus, in her left hand a bilva fruit;

the Goddess, seated in the center of the lotus, smiles upon both sides," one should worship with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, reciting: *oṃ hrīṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*, and then offer this prayer:

"O Lakṣmī! For the sake of pacifying obstacles in this direction, you must remain attentive until the end of the sacrifice, by the command of Śiva. Having thus addressed Lakṣmī, [he addresses] Brāhmī and the others in the same manner.

Having fully worshipped the ten world-protectors (*daśalokapāla*), one should thereafter worship the ten weapons, beginning with the *khaṭvāṅga*, in the directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast. In the east: The *khaṭvāṅga* has two eyes, a human form, and a dark-blue luster; its head is adorned with a sword, and it possesses a cruel gaze. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the *khaṭvāṅga*, hūṃ phaṇ namaḥ.
In the southeast (Agni)—the divine trident, whose body is dark blue, having one face, two eyes, and always holding a river with its two hands. *Oṃ hrīṃ triśūlāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
(L. 5) In the south—having one face and two eyes, holding a bell, and white in form.
And [the deity] Hasta, two-legged, adorned with all ornaments. Oṃ hrīṃ ghaṇṭāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. (l.
6) In the southwest—Nārāca, in human form, dark-complexioned, in the full bloom of youth, one-faced, two-eyed, two-legged, and seated upon a lotus. Oṃ hrīṃ nārācāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
In the west: [the deity] Ḍamaru, having the luster of black color, with one face and two eyes, endowed with a great sound, and adorned with all ornaments. Oṃ hrīṃ ḍamarukāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
In the northwest—[there is] a skull in human form, endowed with a black color, adorned with all ornaments, and beautiful in all its limbs. Oṃ hrīṃ kapālāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
In the north—[there is] a banner indeed in human form, with one face and great strength.
One should resort [to the deity] in the north-eastern direction, two cubits [in height] and two feet [in length]. *Oṃ hrīṃ dhvajāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
In the Īśāna [corner]: a Vetāla, human in form, equipped with a sword and a *kaṭaka*, possessing terrible fangs, white in color, and of great strength. *Oṃ hrīṃ vetālāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*.
To the south of Vetāla: Kṣurika, of fierce form, with two eyes and two feet, endowed with a blue complexion; by him, all enemies shall be destroyed. Oṃ hrīṃ kṣurikāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
To the north of Nārāca: [the deity] has the form of a serpent at the nose, and above that, the form of a man.

To the north, however, is that belonging to Nairṛta, provided with seven nooses for the stake: *oṃ hrīṃ pāśāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Having worshipped all [the deities] with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth.

Thereafter, the Guru, having first taken up the *vardhanī* vessel for the *pāśupatāstra*, and then having had the disciple invoke the *pāśupatāstra-kumbha*, pours an unbroken stream of water from the neck of the *vardhanī* vessel into the front of the jar, step by step, while reciting the root mantra: *oṃ ślīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, while meditating upon the weapon-deity (*astra-durga*) and [the deity] Īśāna... [who is] peaceful.

"For the sake of protecting the sacrifice and for the purpose of destroying obstacles, O guardians of the world, you must remain concentrated and protect my face. Having spoken thus, he circumambulates and, having established the primary pitcher (*kumbha*) in its place on the seat, he subsequently establishes the *vardhanī* pitcher.

Having conceived a firm seat for both the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*, it is as follows: *Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti; oṃ, salutation to Antāsanā; oṃ, salutation to Dharmakanda; oṃ, salutation to Jñānanāla.*

Oṃ, homage to the filaments of dispassion (*vairāgya-kesara*). Oṃ, homage to the pericarp of sovereignty (*aiśvarya-karṇikā*). Oṃ, homage to the lotus seat (*padmāsana*). Oṃ, homage to the bull (*vṛṣabha*). Oṃ, homage to the seat of the *pāśupata* weapon (*pāśupatāstrāsana*). Having thus worshipped the seat, one should perform the meditation: [He is] five-faced, most terrible, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
deformed, sun-like, and fierce, with tawny eyebrows, beard, and hair.
Holding in his hands a sword, a spear, an iron arrow, a bow, a bowstring, a water-pot,
a javelin, a trident, and an axe, as well as a staff.

Having meditated [upon him], the wise one should worship the god Pāśupata along with his limbs. (l.4) Having thus meditated—having installed the form [of the deity] in the water-pot with: *oṃ hāṃ pāśupatāstramūrttaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*—and having performed the invocation and other rites with: *oṃ ślīṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*, [one should proceed with: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hīṃ śirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hūṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ haiṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (p.26a, f.21b, l.1)

Oṃ hauṃ, homage to the eyes, huṃ phaṭ namas. Oṃ haḥ, homage to the weapon, huṃ phaṭ namas. Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), and having carried out the protection, the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the root mantra, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth. Then, having placed [the vessel] upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the Vardhanī on the left side, one should worship the Support Power (*ādhāraśakti*).

Meditation—having meditated upon the goddess Āstreśvarī, who is red in color, with blazing hair, and holding a sword and a shield, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (l. 4) Having thus meditated, [one should offer oblations] into the *vardhanī* vessel: *oṃ hrīṃ pāśupatāstramūrtiśaktaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hrāṃ hṛdayāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hrīṃ śirase huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hrūṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*; *oṃ hraiṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. (ll. 5–6)

Oṃ hrauṃ, homage to the eyes, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ hraḥ, homage to the weapon, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), and having performed the protection, the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) by means of the root-mantra of Śakti, one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth.

"Oṃ hauṃ srauṃ, salutations to Śiva and Śakti. Having said this, touching the *kumbha* with the thumb while forming the *liṅgamudrā*, and touching the *vardhanī* with the fist, one should say: "Salutations to you, O Umā, who possesses the form of the *bhaga*, and to Śaṅkara, who bears the form of the *liṅga*. Salutations to you today! For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this is your immovable form. This is your thirty-fold knowledge; accept it along with your own weapon."

"O Lords, come forth with certainty out of compassion for those devoted to protection"—having thus proclaimed this, and having placed the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) in the pitcher for the sake of protection; having offered the sword of knowledge into the left hand of the deity with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; having recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) as much as possible and offered it into the pitcher; and having recited the root of power (*śaktimūla*) ten times that amount and placed it in the *vardhanī* vessel:
"This sacrifice has been commenced by me; you must protect the performer until its completion. As long as we remain here, [protect us]."

Having thus made this request and offered the *arghya* for cessation (*nirodha*), one should place that vessel right there without moving it. In the northwest, northeast, and eastern *vardhanī*, [one should worship] the goddess who has four arms, two eyes, and the luster of a blue lotus petal;
she holds a noose and a goad, and is accompanied by a full jar and a lotus.

One should meditate upon her who wears yellow garments and deludes the world. *Oṃ klīṃ mohinyai namaḥ*. Having worshipped [her] with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, one should worship the seven Gurus in the pitcher to the west of Durgā in the northeast: *Oṃ sadāśivagurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ anantagurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ śrīkaṇṭhagurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ ambikāgurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ guhagurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ viṣṇugurave namaḥ*; *Oṃ dhātṛgurave namaḥ*.

Having thus worshipped the seven gurus, one should meditate upon the supreme, peaceful Guru: [him] richly adorned with a crown of matted locks, his body white with ashes, joined by a yogic belt over the navel region with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and performing the mudrā known as *kṛtayoga*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the gurus.
"O God of gods, O Lord of the world, O cause of the world's joy!

This [person], having taken refuge in Śiva, offers salutations to You, the Knower. Having thus informed the Guru, and then standing to the south of the altar, one should worship the vessels containing water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, including the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), upon the altar. Alternatively, there may be a single vessel for the water for the feet, the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the guest-offering.

Having washed the vessels with the *astra* mantra, one should place them upon the stand (*sthalikā*). Having placed the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) on the right and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) on the left, and having set out the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) in the middle, one should worship the three types [of water] in sequence: "Oṃ, obeisance to Bhūmi" upon the base of the vessel; "Oṃ, obeisance to Māyā" at the rim of the vessel; and "Oṃ, obeisance to the form of the Sun (*sūryamūrti*)" upon the ring.

Having worshipped the presiding deities with "Oṃ Haḥ, obeisance to Amṛtaśakti" at the top [of the vessel], one should again worship the presiding deities of the *ācamana* vessel as follows: "Oṃ, obeisance to Dhāriṇī" on the base of the vessel; "Oṃ, obeisance to Yoginī" at the rim of the vessel; "Oṃ, obeisance to Somamūrti" on the ring; and "Oṃ, obeisance to Amṛtaśakti" at the top. Then, between those two, on the three-legged stand: "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā," "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," and "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra"; on the circular base: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti"; and above that, at the base of the conch: "Oṃ, obeisance to Dhārādevī."
In the belly: *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. In the channel: *oṃ aghorāya namaḥ*. In the coil: *sūryāya namaḥ*. In the mouth: *saptatīrthāya namaḥ*.

At the entrance: *oṃ candrāya namaḥ*. Having filled those [channels] with water from the *amṛtabindu* with the right hand, [one offers] the foot-water (*pādya*) with the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*).

Having consecrated the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the *pañcabrahma* mantra and the *pañcabrahma-ṣaḍaṅga*, and having consecrated the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), one should consecrate the *śivagāyatrī* over them. Having performed the protection and veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) and rendered [the offerings] nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*, one should present incense and lamps. Thereafter, on the right side of the deity, one should perform the *nirodhārghya*, the *svāgatārghya*, and the *parāṅmukhārghya* along with their respective substances, together with the previously mentioned *viśeṣārghya*. Having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) according to the method prescribed in the mantras—[as stated] in the *Kāmika*: "At the time of installing the Goddess, [one should worship] Śakti, whose form is the support (*ādhārarūpiṇīm*)."

Then, having arranged an inner seat, and above that a lion-throne, with coverings above and below upon the *yogapadma*—without [the petals] starting from the left—one should visualize the three mandalas by means of the powers of action (*kriyā*), will (*icchā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*). Then, one should worship the seat of the Goddess, which is the power that covers what is above that; for example, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) situated upon an altar.

Below [is] the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti), seated upon the Tortoise-stone, her body white as the Ocean of Milk; in her crown is the form of a seed-sprout; she bestows boons and fearlessness; she holds a noose and a goad; she is Śakti, the Kriyā-śakti, whose nature is the foundation. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti*. Above that is the Root of Earth (Pṛthvīkanda), with the tip of its digits as its single stalk and the elements as its thorns.

This is the seat of Ananta, possessing the luster of yellow orpiment, consisting of a great lotus of agitated māyā crowded with many petals. In its center is the region of Āgama, where the Lord stands pervading from below.

One should meditate upon [the deity] as white, four-faced, eight-armed, and twelve-eyed, within the center of the Brahma-stone; one should worship the God upon the Śiva-seat. In the center of the pericarp: *oṃ hāṃ ananteśāya namaḥ*. In the petals of the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ vāsukaye namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ takṣakāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kārkoṭaka. In the petals of the directions beginning with the southeast: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padma; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahāpadma;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śaṅkhā; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Guḷika; Oṃ, homage to Anantāsana. Ananta is said to be the seat, and above that is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
Visualizing them as resembling variegated lions, each looking back at the other,
and each surrounded by a retinue of ten million lions;
and remembering them in the form of beautiful lions, white like saffron and red like *ālī* flowers.

Dharma-knowledge, dispassion, and likewise sovereignty—these are to be placed in the corners starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast, respectively. (Verse 5) In the corners beginning with the southeast: *oṃ hāṃ dharmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ jñānāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ vairāgyāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*.
Their limbs resemble crystal; they possess three eyes and bear lion heads.
Their arms, heads, and necks are rigid, and their crowns are fixed with sandals.
One should worship those presiding over ignorance, unrighteousness, and so forth, while meditating on them as having human forms with heads resting upon their feet and forebodies;
[in the directions] starting from the east: *oṃ hāṃ adharmāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ ajñānāya namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to non-detachment; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to lack of sovereignty.
Thus, by means of the three qualities, the lion-throne is established.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of the Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa [qualities]; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lion-throne.
Thus the lion throne is described; above that is the yoga seat.
That which is called Kṛta is white in color, while Tretā is red at its base.
One should visualize Dvāpara as black in color and Kali as yellow in color;
in the corners beginning with the southeast, one should contemplate the forms of the elements.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kṛta Yuga. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Tretā Yuga. (l.
3) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Dvāpara Yuga. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Kali Yuga. [The principles] beginning with Niyati have the luster of unmanifest crystal, while Kāla is like collyrium. (l. 4)

The radiance of Kālī is like that of a pomegranate flower, with a luster resembling split collyrium. Keśava is said to be the bud at the center, while in the directions starting from the east: *oṃ hāṃ avyaktāya namaḥ*. (l. 5–6)
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Niyati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kāla. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalā.
On the middle foot, obeisance to Keśava. One should contemplate the face below as dark, and those above as red and white.

In the south-western direction and the northeastern quarter is the supreme [seat] consisting of *māyā* and *vidyā*. In the south-west: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the downward-facing *candana* (sandalwood seat).
In the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the upward-facing *candana*. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the *yogāsana*.
Thus the *yogāsana* is described; above that is the *padmāsana*.
The Māyātattva is the great bulbous root, adorned with the lotus of Śuddhavidyā;
it is covered by the petals of the Vidyeśvaras and endowed with the filaments of Śakti.
Therein, one should fashion the pericarp consisting of the Vidyātattva.
The bulb is like a ruby, and the sprout has a reddish luster;
its stalk is indeed lapis lazuli, and the bud is dark-colored.

The thorn is known to have the luster of coral, with a reddish-brown hue like that of the *karṇikāra* flower; its petal-tips are the color of a conch shell, and its sub-petals are red. The filament has the brilliance of gold and is shaped like a pearl at its tip. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the bulb (*kanda*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seed (*bīja*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sprout (*aṅkura*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the stalk (*nāla*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the bud (*mukuḷa*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the thorns (*kaṇṭaka*).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the petals (daḷa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the sub-petals (upadaḷa).
Thus, having meditated upon and worshipped the petals as being the forms of the eight Vidyeśvaras, [one says]: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the filaments (keśara).
Then one should worship the pericarp (*karṇikā*), which has the luster of molten gold, contains fifty seeds, and possesses sixty-four filaments (*kesara*). [One should worship with:
*Oṃ hāṃ karṇikāyai namaḥ*; *Oṃ hāṃ bījebhyo namaḥ*. One should also worship the lotus in its fully manifested form within the pericarp.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lotus posture (*padmāsana*). Thus the lotus posture is described; above it is the pure seat (*vimalāsana*).

One should arrange three mandalas right here as the pure seat: upon the circle at the tip of the petals, conjoined with the twelve digits (*kalā*), there is the mandala of Śiva-Sūrya, resembling ten million suns. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the solar mandala (*sūryamaṇḍala*).
To the sovereign of the solar disc, Oṃ Hrīṃ Jñānaśakti, obeisance!
And in the very center of the pericarp, she possesses a radiance as white as cow’s milk.
One should worship the circle of Śakti, which consists of knowledge and bliss.
(1.2) Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the circle of Śakti; to the sovereign of the circle of Śakti, Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādiśakti.
(1.3) [It is] radiant like the lion-throne of mantras, extending from the earth element up to the limit of Kuṭilā. (1.4)
One should visualize the seat of the Goddess as having a brilliance equal to ten million suns. *Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the seat of Manonmanī.* (p.
1) Having placed a handful of flowers upon that [seat] at the region of the heart, [one recites]: *Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Manonmanī.* (l. 2)
Having thus uttered the [mantra] ending in *viṅ*, one should contemplate the form (*mūrti*) as the complete supreme light, rod-shaped (*daṇḍākārā*), with undivided limbs,
consisting of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*), pervaded by the supreme point (*parabindu*), and having the nature of knowledge and action.

One should place [the deities] within the three maṇḍalas. In this form, having performed the placement starting from the head down to the feet, and starting from Īśāna and so forth, according to the arrangement of the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅgī*):
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the head, and Ambikā. Oṃ hreṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the face, and Gaṇāmbikā. Oṃ hruṃ, obeisance to Aghora, the heart, and Gaṅgā.
Oṃ hriṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, the secret organ, and Gaurī. Oṃ hraṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta and Umā. Having thus performed the placement.
Immediately thereafter, one should deposit the digits of Gaurī according to the method of artistic arrangement (*kalābhaṅgī*), as follows:
on the head, *oṃ hrīṃ tārāyai namaḥ*; on the face, *oṃ hrīṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*; on the heart, *oṃ hrīṃ muninyai namaḥ*;
on the ear, *oṃ hrīṃ śuddhāyai namaḥ*; on the right shoulder, *oṃ hrīṃ rajāyai namaḥ*; on the left shoulder, *oṃ hrīṃ medhāyai namaḥ*.
In the stomach: oṃ hrīṃ svadhāyai namaḥ. In the navel: oṃ hrīṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ. In the womb: oṃ hrīṃ pālinyai namaḥ.
In the secret place: oṃ hrīṃ jvālinyai namaḥ.

On the right thigh: *oṃ hrīṃ tṛṣṇāyai namaḥ*. On the left thigh: *oṃ hrīṃ dhṛtyai namaḥ*. On the right knee: *oṃ hrīṃ kalāyai namaḥ*. On the left knee: *oṃ hrīṃ prajāyai namaḥ*. (l. 3) On the right shank: *oṃ hrīṃ cintāyai namaḥ*. On the left shank: *oṃ hrīṃ bhūtyai namaḥ*. On the back: *oṃ hrīṃ kriyāyai namaḥ*. (l. 4)
On the right side: *oṃ hrīṃ kṣāntyai namaḥ*. On the left side: *oṃ hrīṃ śāntyai namaḥ*. On the right hand: *oṃ hrīṃ smṛtyai namaḥ*.
On the left hand: *oṃ hrīṃ dityai namaḥ*. On the right breast: *oṃ hrīṃ dvityai namaḥ*. On the left breast: *oṃ hrīṃ sāddhyai namaḥ*. Having thus performed the Gaurī-kalā-nyāsa—
To one who is capable, Śiva is with parts (*sakala*), yet he is also known as partless (*niṣkala*).
[One should meditate on her] seated upon the lion-throne of mantra, beginning with the earth and ending with the crooked [final element],
resembling a sapphire, and endowed with the thirty-two auspicious marks.
One should visualize her seated in the lotus posture, three-eyed, radiant with youth,
possessing large eyes, endowed with the digit of the moon of knowledge,
girt with a serpent as a sacred thread, and clad in variegated garments.
Having thus meditated upon Manonmanī, who is endowed with perfumes and garlands and bestows desired objects, one should perform all ritual actions.

Alternatively—having meditated as previously described—one should offer a handful of flowers while reciting: "Oṃ sauṃ, obeisance to the one whose body is the Vidyā; [obeisance] to the Praisāda that pervades up to Śakti."
Having meditated on [the goddess] appearing like a flash of lightning, having projected the *vidyā-deha* in its fully manifested form upon the *bimba*, and having projected the eyes with "Oṃ srauṃ,

homage to the eyes," one should thereafter, with the upper body erect, fill the hands joined in *añjali* with flowers, place them at the region of the heart, and recite the root mantra: "Oṃ hyauṃ, homage to Manonmanī."

Having recited [the mantra] up to the *dvādaśānta* by way of the sequence of Brahmā and the other causal deities, one should contemplate her as the universal self (*sarvātmikā*), partless (*niṣkala*), all-pervading (*vibhu*), consisting of knowledge and bliss (*jñānānandamayī*), and self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*).

Then, by way of the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), having brought her down from the *dvādaśānta* to the forehead—she who has the yellowish-brown luster of a sunbeam—one should meditate on the mandala as white as ten million moons and as pale as nectar, extending obliquely.

Having emerged through the path of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and contemplated her as residing within the hollowed palms (*añjali*), one should invoke her into the heart-lotus of the image of the deity (*lakṣamūrti*) by means of the *āvahinī* mudrā, and perform the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth.
Having offered a welcome and the *arghya* water, and having announced, "Welcome, O Great Goddess," one should contemplate Gaurī saying, "Welcome, my child.
Then [one recites]: "O Gaurī, O Sovereign of the Entire World, until the conclusion of the worship..."

"Remain present within this jar with a state of affection for that long. Having thus informed [the deity], [one should worship] in the locations beginning with the heart and ending with the hands: Oṃ srāṃ, obeisance to Hṛdayavāsinī (She who Dwell in the Heart). Oṃ srīṃ, obeisance to Śiraḥnīlinī (She who Is Blue at the Head).

Oṃ srūṃ, obeisance to Śikhācakriṇī (She who Bears the Wheel on the Topknot). Oṃ sraiṃ, obeisance to Kavacapāśāṅgī (She whose Limbs Are the Armor and the Noose). Oṃ srauṃ, obeisance to Netrakhaṭvāṅgī (She who Bears the Sword and the Khatvāṅga as Her Eyes).

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) with "Oṃ sraḥ, salutation to the Gāmbhīryā-weapon," having established oneness [with the deity] by means of the root mantra, having protected it with the weapon mantra, and having concealed it with the armor mantra;

(l. 4) having displayed the cow-seal (*dhenumudrā*), the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), the lotus seal (*padmamudrā*), the trident seal (*śūlamudrā*), and the womb-seal (*yonimudrā*) by means of the root mantra; having offered water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*) to the Śakti by means of the root mantra; (l. 5) having worshipped her with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; then, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel in the left portion, one should offer flowers and consecrated rice (*akṣata*) with "Oṃ hrīṃ"; having offered the food offering (*naivedya*), incense (*dhūpa*), and lamps (*dīpa*), and having displayed the wish-fulfilling seal (*manorathamudrā*). (l. 6)

Having worshipped [the deity] with the root-mantra of the Śakti, one should then meditate upon the seat of the Pīṭha-Śakti in the Vardhanī on the left side, reciting: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of the Pīṭha-Śakti; Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the form of the Pīṭha-Śakti.

The wise practitioner should meditate upon Pīṭhaśakti, who has two eyes and two arms, is yellow in complexion, and is endowed with white garments; she is adorned with a jeweled casket crown and decorated with all ornaments, seated comfortably upon her throne. [He should worship her] with *oṃ hrīṃ pīṭhaśaktyai namaḥ*, along with food offerings, incense, lamps, and other articles.
Having performed the worship [of the central deity], one should thereafter worship Vāmā and the others. In the east: *oṃ hrīṃ vāmāsanāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ hrīṃ vāmamūrttaye namaḥ*.
[One should visualize] the goddess Vāmā, blue in luster, adorned with a crown and celestial ornaments.
The wise practitioner should likewise meditate upon her as bearing the conch and the discus. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to Vāmā in the southeast;
*Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhāsanā; *Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhamūrti.
One should meditate on Jyeṣṭhā, who has a yellow complexion, holds a lotus, and has lotus-like eyes.
Adorned with all ornaments, well-placed, and in the full bloom of youth. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhā.
To the Southern [Direction]: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Raudryāsanā; Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Raudrimūrti.

And [one should worship] Raudrī, who has a white-blue luster, is three-eyed, and holds a trident; she is adorned with a basket-shaped crown and clothed in yellow garments. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Raudrī in the southwest—Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the seat of Kālī; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the form of Kālī.
[One should worship] the Goddess who resembles molten gold, who holds a black mace, who is clothed in fine silk garments, and who is adorned with all ornaments. *Oṃ hrīṃ kālyai namaḥ* (in the west).
*Oṃ hrīṃ kalavikaraṇyāsanāya namaḥ*. *Oṃ hrīṃ kalavikaraṇīmūrtaye namaḥ*.

[One should meditate upon] Kalavikaraṇī, who is red in color, holds a noose in her hand, possesses great strength, is endowed with full breasts, and is adorned with red garlands. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī.
In the northwest (Vāyu): Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the seat of Balavikariṇī; Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the form of Balavikariṇī.
And [I worship] Balavikariṇī, who has a white body, who holds a sword and a shield, who wears red garments, and who possesses a serene countenance. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to Balavīkaraṇī.
In the north: *Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the seat of Balapramathanī; *oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to the form of Balapramathanī.

(L.3) One should meditate upon the goddess Balapramathanī, whose radiance is like a dark blue cloud, who is adorned with a crown of matted hair, and who holds a noose and a staff. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, obeisance to Balapramathinī. (L.4)
In the northeast: *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to the seat of Sarvabhūtadamani; *oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to the form of Sarvabhūtadamani.

And [one should meditate on] Sarvabhūtadamani, who is red in color and in the full bloom of youth, possessing great heroism with a spear in her hand, and adorned with a crown and other ornaments. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamani.

Having worshipped all with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, he then worships the principal *vardhanī* vessel with the root mantra, makes his petition, and requests permission to perform the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇapūjā*).
In the northeast petal: *oṃ sroṃ* to Īśāna, the head, and Ambikā, salutation. In the east: *oṃ sreṃ* to Tatpuruṣa, the face, and Gaṇāmbikā, salutation.
In the south: *oṃ srūṃ* to Aghora, the heart, and Gaṅgā, salutation. (l. 3)
In the north: Oṃ srīṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva-Guhyagaurī.
In the west: Oṃ srauṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta-Umā. In the southeast: Oṃ srāṃ, salutation to Hṛdaya-Vāminī.
In the northeast: *oṃ srīṃ*, salutation to Śirānīlinī; in the southwest: *oṃ srūṃ*, salutation to Śikhācakriṇī;
in the northwest: *oṃ sraiṃ*, salutation to Kavacapāśāṅgī.
To the west of Īśāna: *Oṃ srauṃ*, salutation to Netrakhaḍginī.
To the east of Nirṛti: *Oṃ sraḥ*, salutation to Astragāmbhinī.
Having thus worshipped the inner enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*), [one worships] in the second enclosure on the altar, starting from the east and ending at Īśāna, in the Vardhanīs.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Vāmā. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Raudrī. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Kālī.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Balavikaraṇī. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Balapramathanī. Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī.

Having thus completed the worship of the second enclosure, [one worships] in the third enclosure the eight jars situated at the sides of the four gates starting from the east: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śanaiścara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Skanda. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śāstṛ.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvarī.
The third enclosure is to be fully worshipped. In the fourth enclosure, at the eight locations starting from the east, [one offers] to Vardhanī:
*oṃ hrīṃ brāhmyai namaḥ*.

Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī. (l. 3) Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Māhendrī. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Cāmuṇḍā. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Durgā. To the south of Durgā: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī. (l. 4) To the north of Vaiṣṇavī: Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī. Having thus worshipped the fourth enclosure (caturthāvaraṇa). (l. 5)
In the fifth enclosure—in the directions from the east to the northeast—one should worship the ten weapons:
*oṃ khaḍvāṅgāya namaḥ* (homage to the club with a skull); *oṃ triśūlāya namaḥ* (homage to the trident).

Oṃ, salutation to Ghaṇṭā; oṃ, salutation to Nārāca; oṃ, salutation to Ḍamaruka; oṃ, salutation to Kapāla; oṃ, salutation to Dhvaja; (l. 2) oṃ, salutation to Vetāla. To the south of Vetāla, oṃ, salutation to Kṣurikā. To the north of Nārāca, oṃ, salutation to Pāśa. (l.
3) Having thus worshipped the fivefold enclosure, one should thereafter honor the Goddess with eight flowers, and offer water for the feet and so forth, as well as incense and lamps. (l. 4)

Having announced, "I shall perform the fire-rite (*agnikārya*)," and having performed it as prescribed for the fire-rite, one should worship the Goddess at the conclusion of the *homa* with the mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ śivāyai namaḥ*.

Then, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, along with three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), it is as follows: To the Sovereign of the *Ātmatattva*, *Oṃ hrāṃ śivāyai namaḥ*. To the Sovereign of the *Vidyātattva*, *Oṃ hrīṃ śivāyai namaḥ*. To the Sovereign of the *Śivatattva*, *Oṃ hrūṃ śivāyai namaḥ*.

Having thus offered three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should thereafter worship with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), beginning with the food offering (*naivedya*). The procedure for the worship of the pavilion of the Lord’s power (*īśa-śakti-maṇḍapa*) is complete. Hariḥ Oṃ.
The deposition of the female messengers (dūtikānyāsa).

Amṛtā, Āvaivasvatā, Jihvā, Praṇahā, Ārkaṣyā, Granthinī, Pramādā, Visphuliṅginī, Kṣetrā, Pratiharī, Prāṇadūtī, and those beginning with Apsuyā—[these reside] in the heart: Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hoṃ Haṃsaḥ.
Yaṃ Amṛte.

O messenger, come, come! Having entered his heart, having seized even that which is of the same nature—by force, bring, bring the form of his skin! Enter, enter the *bimba* and so forth! Establish, establish! Come back again, come back! Be firm in your own place! *Vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ yaṃ*. Of this supreme Śiva, whose self is the skin, of this supreme Śiva, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is here, the vital breath.

The life-force (*jīva*) of this Supreme Śiva resides here. May all the senses of this Supreme Śiva—speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath—come here and remain happily for a long time. *Svāhā*. *Glauṃ*, paralyze, paralyze! 1.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ*. O messenger of Vaivasvata, come, come! Having entered the heart of this person, seize even his kinsman by force. Of this person...
Bring the form of the *īsṛk*, bring the *bimba* and so forth; enter, enter—establish, establish; come back again, come back—be firm in your own place, *vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.

(l. 5) *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ raṃ*. Of this [person], whose self is the blood of the Supreme Śiva, of this Supreme Śiva, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is here, the vital breath.

The life-force (*jīva*) of this Supreme Śiva resides here. May all the senses of this Supreme Śiva—speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath—come to this very place and remain happily for a long time. *Svāhā*. *Glauṃ*, paralyze, paralyze! 2. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ*. O *Jīva*, come, come, O messenger (*dūtikā*). Having entered the heart of this person, seize even his kinsmen by force. Of this person...

*Laṃ*, bring, bring the form of flesh, the *bimba* and so forth; enter, enter; remain, remain; come back again, come back; be firm in your own place! *Vauṣaṭ namaḥ*. *Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ*. *Laṃ*, the life-force (*jīva*) of this supreme Śiva, whose essence is flesh, of such-and-such [name], is situated here within this supreme Śiva.

The life-breath of that Supreme Śiva comes here; O life-breath! The all the sense-faculties—speech, mind, sight, hearing, tongue, smell, and breath—of that Supreme Śiva, having come right here, may they remain happily for a long time, Svāhā! Glauṃ! Paralyze, paralyze! 3.

Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Ya Ra La Va Śa Ṣa Sa Hoṃ Haṃsaḥ—Vaṃ! O Life-breath, O Messenger, come, come! Having entered the heart of this person and having forcibly seized even his kinsmen, [seize] this person’s...

*Vaṃ*. Bring the form into the fat; bring the image (*bimba*) and so forth; cause it to enter, cause it to enter—cause it to remain, cause it to remain. Return again, return! And be firm in your own place! *Vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.

*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ vaṃ*. Of this [deity] whose nature is non-different from the Supreme Śiva, of this Supreme Śiva, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is here, the vital breath is here.

The life-force (*jīva*) of this Supreme Śiva resides here. May all the senses of this Supreme Śiva—speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and breath—come here and remain happily for a long time. *Svāhā! Glauṃ! Paralyze, paralyze!* 4.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ! O messenger (*dūtī*), come, come! Having entered the heart of this person and having forcibly seized even his kinsmen, [seize] this one...*

May there be well-being. Bring the form, bring it! Cause the image and so forth to enter, cause them to enter! Establish, establish! Return again, return! And remain firm in your own place, *vauṣaṇnamaḥ*.

*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ śaṃ*. Of this [person], who is non-different from the Self of Supreme Śiva—of this Supreme Śiva, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is here, the vital breath is here.

The life-force (*jīva*) of this Supreme Śiva resides here. May all the sense-faculties of this Supreme Śiva—speech, mind, sight, hearing, tongue, smell, and breath—come right here and remain for a long time in happiness, *svāhā*. *Glauṃ*! Paralyze, paralyze! 5.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ*—*Ṣaṃ Granthinī Dūtikā*, come, come! Having entered the heart of this person, having forcibly seized even his kinsmen, [seize] this one... 6.
*Ṣaṃ*, bring the marrow-form, bring it! Enter the *bimba* and so forth, enter! Establish it, establish it! Return again, return! Be firm in your own place, *vauṣaṭ namaḥ*.
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ ṣaṃ*. Of this [person], who is non-different from the Self of Supreme Śiva, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of this Supreme Śiva is here;
the vital breath of this Supreme Śiva is established here. Of this Supreme Śiva, all the sense organs—speech, mind, eye, ear—[are established here].
O tongue, nose, and vital breaths, come here indeed and remain happily for a long time, svāhā! Glauṃ! Paralyze, paralyze! 6.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ—O Messenger (dūtikā), come, come at this moment of negligence! Having entered the heart of such-and-such a person, having seized even his kinsmen by force, bring, bring the white form of such-and-such a person; cause the image and so forth to enter, enter! Establish, establish! Come back again, come back! Be firm in your own place, vauṣaṇnamaḥ! Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ haṃsaḥ—O Saṃ, [seize] the white essence of the supreme Śiva of such-and-such a person.

The breath of this Supreme Śiva is here, O breath; the life-force (*jīva*) of this Supreme Śiva is stationed here.
